LayerNorm can undermine the interpretation that a nearly uniform EWMA produces a weak residual. Let δ=EWMAρ(x)−causal_mean(x), with feature variance v. Without affine parameters, residual RMS is σ(g)√[v/(v+ε)]. Thus v≫ε gives approximately σ(g), regardless of δ’s small magnitude; v≪ε gives approximately σ(g)√(v/ε), which vanishes. Derived from [PyTorch’s LayerNorm formula](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.modules.normalization.LayerNorm.html): for a finite-prefix, normalized EWMA, δ=O(1−ρ), so normalization largely removes this amplitude dependence until the epsilon regime. An unnormalized, zero-initialized EMA need not approach the uniform mean.

Differentiating that formula, the centered-input Jacobian has tangential gain 1/√(v+ε) and radial gain ε/(v+ε)^(3/2). Near zero variance, sensitivity approaches 1/√ε—about 316 for ε=10⁻⁵—before the gate and affine scale. Outside that regime, leading amplitude changes with ρ largely cancel; directional changes remain learnable. Learned γ changes residual strength, and β can leave a nonzero residual at δ=0. These are mathematical deductions; [LayerNorm gradient analysis](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper/8689-understanding-and-improving-layer-normalization.pdf) supports treating backward normalization explicitly.

Stable implementation choices: compute EMA, mean, subtraction, and normalization in FP32; casting after low-precision subtraction cannot recover lost information ([PyTorch numerical guidance](https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/more-in-depth-details-of-floating-point-precision/654)). For normalized causal EWMA, use differentiable recurrences Sₜ=ρSₜ₋₁+xₜ, Zₜ=ρZₜ₋₁+1, mₜ=Sₜ/Zₜ, starting from zero and skipping padding. This avoids dividing by 1−ρᵗ and reaches the uniform mean smoothly. If those factors are required, compute them with −expm1(t·logρ), which improves small-argument accuracy ([documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/special.html)). To preserve weak-residual semantics, use an external small scale with the raw difference, or a fixed reference normalization scale; disable affine bias.
